facts.text: TempleOS was created by Terry A. Davis, who wrote it largely on his own.
facts.note: Both the sole-author claim and its scale are repeated in nearly every account.

facts.text: Terry Davis was born on 15 December 1969.
Terry Davis died on 11 August 2018, aged 48.
TempleOS is a 64-bit operating system for PCs, released into the public domain.
Its display is fixed at 640 by 480 pixels with 16 colours.
facts.note: Davis defended this choice as part of the design.

facts.text: Everything runs in one address space at the highest privilege level (ring 0), with no separation between the kernel and programs.
HolyC is both the programming language and the command-line shell, and the compiler is built into the system.

facts.note: Often cited as a deliberate design choice.

facts.text: It was first called the J Operating System, then LoseThos, then SparrowOS, and renamed TempleOS in 2013.
facts.note: The names and their order are well known; the exact years vary between accounts.

facts.text: Davis said that God told him to build it, and that it was God's temple.
facts.note: These are Davis's own words, and they shaped how he described the project.

facts.text: Its documents use a hypertext format called DolDoc, in which text, links and small pictures can sit inside source code.
The system includes a program called the Oracle (or Word of God) that picks random words, which Davis treated as messages.
Davis was struck by a train and killed.
facts.note: Reported widely; the details are not repeated here.

facts.text: Davis lived with serious mental illness (reports describe schizophrenia), which was part of the story of the project.
facts.note: Described this way in most accounts. Reports differ on the diagnosis and its history.

facts.text: In his later years Davis made many offensive and abusive statements, which are well documented. This site is about the software.
TempleOS is on the order of 100,000 lines of code.
facts.note: A figure often quoted; sources differ.

facts.text: The sound is limited to a single voice.
Davis trained as an electrical engineer and worked as a programmer before his illness.
